prompt: A German electronics company has developed a solar lantern (6 hours of sun gives 8 hours of light for a small room) and wants to know whether to enter the Indian market, mainly rural, and how to achieve the profits. It manufactures and uses third-party distribution. Its selling price is Rs 6000.

clarifying.answer: Profit: estimate the profit from entering and how to achieve it (price, production, distribution, marketing).
Open to all of India but expecting to sell mainly in rural areas.
6 hours of bright sun fully charges it for 8 hours of light; it lasts 2 years and is priced at Rs 6000, roughly Rs 300/month over its life (an EMI plan is assumed, at negligible extra cost).
The client manufactures and outsources distribution to third parties.

facts.note: Market size ~30mn lanterns comes from filtering rural families by affordability: BPL cannot afford (Rs 300/month is ~10% of income against essential needs), ~50% of lower-middle can, and middle-class families average 1.2 lanterns each; ~20% is lost to cheap clones and ~20% of middle class use inverters/generators.

exhibits.title: Affordability by Rural Income Segment
exhibits.unlock_condition: Candidate sizes the market by filtering rural families on affordability and asks for income segments.
exhibits.so_what: BPL families cannot afford the lantern because illumination competes with essential needs; roughly half of lower-middle and all of middle class can, with middle-class families averaging 1.2 lanterns. Affordability, not desire, sets the market.

exhibits.title: Cost as a Share of the Rs 6000 Price
exhibits.unlock_condition: Candidate asks for the cost per unit or the breakdown of cost components to compute profit per unit.
exhibits.so_what: Costs total 90% of the Rs 6000 price (Rs 5400), leaving Rs 600 profit per lantern. That per-unit profit drives the entry economics.

phases.name: opening
phases.interviewer_instructions: State the prompt. Wait for the candidate to restate the entry decision and set profit as the metric, planning both the profit estimate and how to achieve it.

coaching.explain: A strong candidate frames two questions: what profit can we expect (size x share x profit per unit), and how do we achieve it (production, distribution, marketing, and whether a JV is needed).
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Restate: 'I'll estimate expected profit as market size x share x profit per unit, then work through production, distribution and marketing to see if we can actually achieve it.'

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate frames both the profit estimate and the how-to-achieve-it path.

phases.name: structuring
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask for the plan. Look for expected profit = market size x market share x profit per unit, plus a second branch on execution (production, distribution, marketing, JV/acquisition to fix constraints).

coaching.explain: Structure the case as economics (size x share x profit per unit) and execution (production, distribution, marketing). The execution branch is where constraints like limited production capacity will bite.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Split into expected profit (size x share x profit per unit) and how to achieve it (production, distribution, marketing), and plan to test each.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate structures economics plus execution and lists the achievement levers.

phases.name: market-sizing
phases.interviewer_instructions: Release ex1_affordability when the candidate filters rural families by affordability. Guide them: BPL cannot afford, ~50% of lower-middle can, middle class averages 1.2 lanterns. Accept the ~30mn market size.

coaching.explain: Size the market by filtering rural families on whether Rs 300/month is affordable. BPL cannot (essentials dominate income), about half of lower-middle can, and middle-class families average 1.2 lanterns (80% buy one, 20% buy two). This filtering yields a market of about 30mn lanterns.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Filter rural families by income affordability, compute 1.2 lanterns per buying middle-class family, and reach ~30mn lanterns.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate filters rural families by affordability (excluding BPL) to reach ~30mn lanterns.

phases.name: market-share
phases.interviewer_instructions: Have the candidate examine substitutes with no direct competitor: temporary ones (torches, candles) are dismissed; inverters/generators take ~20% of middle class; cheap clones (Rs 600, 6-month life) take share. Reward the point that differentiation limits, but does not erase, clone losses.

coaching.explain: There is no direct competitor, so map substitutes. Torches and candles are temporary and dismissed; inverters/generators serve ~20% of middle class; cheap clones (Rs 600, poor quality) are the real threat. Differentiation (hallmark, awareness, service) limits but does not erase clone losses, say a 20% share loss.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Dismiss temporary substitutes, net out inverter users and a ~20% clone share loss after differentiation, to land on an achievable share.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate maps substitutes, dismisses the temporary ones, and nets clone and inverter losses to an achievable share.

phases.name: math
phases.interviewer_instructions: Release ex2_cost_structure when asked for cost per unit. Guide: cost is 90% of Rs 6000 = Rs 5400, profit Rs 600/unit; expected profit 30mn x Rs 600 = Rs 1800 Cr; but production is capped at half, so profit caps at Rs 900 Cr. Verdicts come from the math checker.

coaching.explain: Cost components sum to 90% of the Rs 6000 price = Rs 5400, so profit is Rs 600/unit. At 30mn lanterns that is Rs 1800 Cr. But the client can only produce half (15mn), so profit is capped at 15mn x Rs 600 = Rs 900 Cr. Since production, not competition, is the binding constraint, clones actually matter less.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: Compute Rs 600 profit per unit, Rs 1800 Cr uncapped, then apply the production cap to Rs 900 Cr and note production is the binding constraint.

phases.pass_criteria: Candidate computes Rs 600/unit, Rs 1800 Cr uncapped, and the Rs 900 Cr production-capped profit.

phases.name: synthesis
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask for the recommendation. Look for: enter, expect ~Rs 900 Cr limited by production (so consider expanding capacity or a JV), piggyback distribution on torch/electronics channels, differentiate from clones with local sales and service, and a risk.

coaching.explain: Enter: even production-capped, profit is ~Rs 900 Cr. The binding constraint is capacity, so the real lever is expanding production (or a JV/acquisition), not fighting clones. Piggyback distribution on existing torch and basic-electronics channels, and use local salesmen for awareness, differentiation, and replacements so the lantern is not a 'risky' buy. Risk: clone share loss and affordability assumptions are subjective, so pilot.
coaching.model_approach_for_phase: 'Enter: profit is ~Rs 900 Cr even at half capacity, and since production is the binding constraint, expanding capacity or partnering matters more than clones. Distribute via existing torch/electronics channels and use local sales and service to differentiate. Risk: the clone and affordability assumptions are soft, so pilot a region first.'

phases.pass_criteria: Recommendation is to enter, names production as the binding constraint (expand/JV), sorts distribution and differentiation, and notes a risk.

common_errors: Assuming the shares should sum to 100% including profit
Applying the 10% profit share as cost
Taking 10% of cost rather than of price
Averaging 1 and 2 to 1.5 instead of weighting 80/20
Dropping a zero converting to crores
Forgetting the production cap and using 30mn
Halving the profit per unit instead of the volume

curveballs.injected_fact: Suppose a local partner could double your production capacity through a joint venture, but would take 30% of the profit. Is it worth it? (Strong answer: doubling capacity lifts uncapped profit toward Rs 1800 Cr; even giving up 30% leaves ~Rs 1260 Cr, well above the Rs 900 Cr solo cap, so yes, subject to partner reliability.)

model_answer.framework: Expected profit = market size x market share x profit per unit, paired with an execution branch (production, distribution, marketing). Market size is an affordability-filtered rural estimate; profit per unit comes from the cost structure; production capacity is the binding constraint.
key_insights: Affordability, not desire, sizes the market: BPL cannot afford it, ~50% of lower-middle and all middle class can, giving ~30mn lanterns.
There is no direct competitor; cheap clones are the real share threat, limited but not erased by differentiation.
Cost is 90% of the Rs 6000 price, leaving Rs 600 profit per unit, so 30mn lanterns imply Rs 1800 Cr.
Production is capped at 15mn, so profit caps at Rs 900 Cr, making capacity, not competition, the binding constraint.
model_answer.recommendation: Enter: even production-capped profit is about Rs 900 Cr. Because capacity is the binding constraint, prioritise expanding production or a JV over fighting clones; distribute by piggybacking on existing torch and electronics channels; and use local salesmen for awareness, differentiation and replacements so the lantern is a safe purchase. Pilot a region first, since the clone and affordability assumptions are soft.
model_answer.walkthrough: Frame economics plus execution, size the market by rural affordability to ~30mn, net substitutes and clones to an achievable share, compute Rs 600/unit and Rs 1800 Cr uncapped, apply the production cap to Rs 900 Cr, and recommend entering with capacity expansion as the priority.

anchors.1: No entry structure; a yes/no with no profit or execution logic.
anchors.3: Uses size x share x profit per unit but omits the execution/constraint branch.
anchors.5: Structures economics plus execution and anticipates the production constraint.

anchors.1: Cannot compute profit per unit or apply the production cap.
anchors.3: Computes profit per unit and uncapped profit but misses the production cap.
anchors.5: Computes Rs 600/unit, Rs 1800 Cr uncapped, and the Rs 900 Cr production cap cleanly.

anchors.1: Sizes the market on desire, ignoring affordability, or ignores clones entirely.
anchors.3: Handles affordability or substitutes but not the insight that production is the binding constraint.
anchors.5: Sizes by affordability, nets clones sensibly, and sees capacity (not clones) as the real constraint.

anchors.1: Rambling or silent; cannot convey the layered filtering.
anchors.3: Explains steps but does not narrate the affordability and substitute logic.
anchors.5: Clearly narrates affordability sizing, substitute netting, and the capacity insight.

anchors.1: No recommendation, or 'enter' with no constraint or execution plan.
anchors.3: Recommends entering but omits the capacity constraint or the distribution/differentiation plan.
anchors.5: Recommends entering, prioritises capacity expansion, sorts distribution and differentiation, and names a risk.
